verdict.rationale: FireHydrant documents a full API that it says can do "anything you can do on the FireHydrant UI." It authenticates with API keys that act like a user, plus bot tokens for non-human callers, and it has an official MCP server for its API. Together these give an agent a plausible dashboard-free path to incident lifecycle actions. However, the evidence never shows the specific acknowledge, escalate, and resolve operations through the API or MCP, so the end-to-end loop rests on a broad parity claim. missing for 10: explicitly documented acknowledge/escalate/resolve endpoints or MCP tools, an end-to-end agent workflow example, independent or hands-on corroboration of MCP-driven incident handling.

support.subject: As an AI-native user, my agent can acknowledge, escalate, and resolve incidents end to end through a documented API or MCP connection — no dashboard in the loop

citations.quote: You can use the FireHydrant API to configure integrations, define incidents, and set up webhooks--anything you can do on the FireHydrant UI.
An API key can perform actions like any other user, and by default, it will have Owner permissions.
FireHydrant supports bot tokens to act on behalf of a computer instead of a user's account.
An MCP server for interacting with FireHydrant's API.
